extracted.intended_audience: students attending Cambridge Analysis I (first-year undergraduate analysis) and similar undergraduate analysis learners
extracted.subtask_short: Analysis I course learning and proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for learning/teaching Cambridge's Analysis I course: how to study, how to understand and memorise proofs, how to approach Tripos-style problems, and a few technical tips (e.g., for power series and Taylor's theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be comfortable with basic logic
rubrics_metrics.description: You will find this course much easier to understand if you are comfortable with basic logic. In particular, you should be clear about what 'implies' means and should not be afraid of the quantifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review basic logic material before or alongside the course; see the author's earlier posts about logic. Comfort with quantifiers and implication is stated as foundational for the course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimise rote memorisation of proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempt to learn proofs while making as little use of your memory as possible — aim for an understanding that avoids memorising long strings of symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make your memory of a proof like a pattern (example: 5432187654321 is seen as two counting-down patterns). Learn the repetitive/obvious steps and only retain the few genuinely non-obvious steps, and when you do retain them, understand why they are sensible so they become natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solve proofs by repeatedly doing the obvious thing; isolate small non-obvious steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Analysis I proofs are 'easy' in the sense that repeatedly doing the obvious thing will solve them; some require one small idea when the obvious steps run out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working through a proof, carry out the straightforward steps until you reach a point requiring a small insight; focus effort on understanding that insight rather than memorising ad hoc tricks. As you gain experience previously 'clever' steps should become natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: When answering exam/Tripos questions, state any properties you use
rubrics_metrics.description: If a question asks you to use the integral or to assume standard properties, state clearly any properties of the integral (or other objects) that you require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the question's instructions (e.g., 'You are not asked to prove existence'). If allowed to assume standard properties (for example, of cosine), explicitly state those assumptions so examiners know what you are using.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the question constraints and instructions carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay attention to wording such as 'State without proof', 'You are not asked to prove existence', or other limits specified by the question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor your answer to what is requested — do not add unnecessary proofs or omit required statements. Use exactly the level of justification the problem asks for and make any assumed facts explicit when permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know precise definitions used in course/quizzes
rubrics_metrics.description: Quizzes and questions may expect precise definitions (example: the quiz on continuity expects you to know the definitions of adherent points and limit points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure you can state and use the exact definitions of terms covered in lectures and quizzes; gaps in these definitions are common sources of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use short quizzes to diagnose weak areas
rubrics_metrics.description: A short multiple-choice quiz (e.g., Vicky Neale's quiz or Terence Tao's quizzes) is a good way to test basic knowledge and to identify areas needing attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you don't get every question right first time, use the quiz results to guide revision. Quizzes can pinpoint specific conceptual gaps to focus on.

rubrics_metrics.name: When proving differentiability of power series, show convergence of the termwise differentiated series
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a power series is differentiable inside its circle of convergence and that its derivative is given by the termwise-differentiated series, one must show the series of termwise derivatives converges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical approach is to compare the series to a geometric progression and use the ratio test: inside the circle of convergence the original series converges at least as fast as a GP, and multiplying the nth term by n does not prevent convergence (so the differentiated series still converges). Make these convergence comparisons explicit in the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer transparent, conceptual proofs (e.g., for Taylor's theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek proofs that make the structure transparent and minimise ad hoc memorisation (the author prefers an approach to Taylor's theorem that generalises the mean value theorem idea rather than using Cauchy's mean value theorem as a black box).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, find proofs that are natural generalisations of basic theorems you understand (e.g., viewing Taylor's theorem as a polynomial mean value theorem). Such proofs reduce memory load and improve understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: When allowed, explicitly state standard assumptions you invoke
rubrics_metrics.description: If a problem permits you to assume standard properties (for example, standard properties of the cosine function), explicitly state those properties when you use them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This makes your argument clearer and acceptable in an exam setting; do not silently use unstated facts even if they are 'standard'.
